newsitem.title: USA: House Conservatives deny seeking Gingrich ouster.
newsitem.headline: House Conservatives deny seeking Gingrich ouster.

text.p: A group of Republican critics of U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich reviewed recent public setbacks to their conservative agenda on Tuesday but denied they intended to bring down their leaders.

Representative Mark Souder, Republican of Indiana, said about 50 representatives were dissatisfied with the Republican leadership's response to President Bill Clinton's veto of the disaster relief bill.

Publicity over Tuesday's invitation-only meeting -- which hinted at a plot to oust Gingrich or other leaders -- was believed to have kept lawmakers away. Organisers rushed to deny any connection with an anonymous letter, which called for a challenge to Gingrich.
"This kind of stuff is not what you take down a speaker over," Souder said of their frustration over the disaster-aid bill. "This is not about the speaker. We need a clear conservative message."

Souder said they were concerned that the conservative message was not being clearly articulated. A delay in sending the disaster-aid bill to the White House gave Clinton three days while they were out of town to blame them for keeping the aid from reaching flood-stricken states.
This is only the latest in a series of problems to plague Gingrich, who barely won re-election as speaker in January and was repimanded and fined by his colleagues for ethics violations.
While there has been speculation that he might step down before the end of his two-year term, he did not show signs of that this week.

"The leadership is fine," Representative David Hobson of Ohio told reporters after a closed meeting in Gingrich's office. Lawmakers said the unhappiness of their conservative wing was not discussed, and they appeared unperturbed as they shared in Gingrich's chocolate birthday cake. He turned 54 today.

Many of those frustrated by the pace and direction of leadership were among the freshmen who were elected in 1994 as part of Gingrich's Republican revolution and remain intent upon cutting the size and cost of government.

In an effort to quell the incipient rebellion, Republican leaders were to stress to their rank-and-file at a Wednesday meeting that the party has made progress on budget issues -- including an agreement to balance the budget in five years, cut taxes and reform entitlement programmes.
